fetched_contents.text: Deterrence vs. gamesmanship: Taxpayer response to targeted audits and endogenous penalties Highlights * • Audit selection and payment rates are endogenous to the amount of evasion. * • A deterrence model that realistically accounts for this predicts far less evasion. * • A taxpayer wants to ensure his preferred outcome even if evasion has a high return. * • Other findings that appear to contradict the classical framework can be explained. * • Calibrations estimate how audit and payment rates relate to the amount of evasion. Abstract Taxpayers with large amounts of non-third-party-reported income usually self-report at least a portion of it, an act inconsistent with common theories of compliance. I explain this behavior by generalizing the classical evasion theory to realistically account for the endogeneity of audit and payment rates. These taxpayers refrain from more evasion not due to deterrence, but to tilt the odds and payoffs of the evasion gamble. The introduction of this incentive helps explain many empirical findings that seemingly contradict a more restrictive and unrealistic version of the “deterrence paradigm.” I also estimate feasible structural calibrations, the first based on observed compliance behavior, of taxpayers’ perceptions of the relationship between evasion, audit probabilities, and payment rates. Introduction The U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) estimates that $450 billion of the $2660 billion federal tax liability for TY2006 went unpaid.1 In response to the 16.3% noncompliance estimate for TY01, Senator Max Baucus stated that the tax gap is “unacceptable”2 and that its elimination “could reduce the deficit by three-fourths …, cover most of the $492 billion in annual Social Security outlays …, [or] completely pay for the $294 billion in annual Medicare costs.”3 In contrast, the standard economic theory of tax evasion leads one to wonder not why the tax gap is so large, but why it is so small. Under this theory taxpayers treat evasion as they would any other gamble and are deterred solely by the risk of being caught and penalized. However, low aggregate measures of audit and penalty rates do not appear sufficient to deter taxpayers from larger-than-observed amounts of noncompliance.4 “Indeed, the puzzle of tax compliance behavior may be why people pay taxes, not why they evade them” (Alm et al., 2010a). This article addresses the compliance puzzle for a particular but important category of taxpayers, namely those with large amounts of unmatched income. “Unmatched” refers to income that is not reported to the tax agency by a corroborating third-party. These taxpayers warrant special attention for two distinct reasons. First, they tend to underreport their unmatched income, but only a portion of it. This is noteworthy because such behavior is not readily explained by the most commonly posited solutions to the tax compliance puzzle. Second, these taxpayers are common in the U.S., underreport relatively large amounts of income on a per capita basis, and contribute disproportionately to the total tax gap.5 This makes an understanding of their behavior all the more pressing and policy-relevant. What are the commonly posited solutions to the tax compliance puzzle, and why do they not explain the behavior of high unmatched income taxpayers? These theories can essentially be categorized as corresponding to “ability” and “willingness” to evade. This nomenclature is borrowed from the title of Kleven et al. (2011), in which “ability” is defined as the possession of “evadable” unmatched income. Taxpayers are largely compliant in self-reporting matched income (i.e. income subject to third-party reporting), but tend to underreport 100% of unmatched income. However, both Kleven et al. (2011) and Phillips (2013) show that the pattern of 100% underreporting holds only for low unmatched income taxpayers, not high unmatched income taxpayers.6 High income taxpayers have the “ability” to evade more tax liability, but do not. “Taking information reporting into account, taxpayers still appear to be more honest than might be expected …” (Andreoni et al., 1998). If “ability” does not do the trick, it is natural to appeal to an explanation that addresses taxpayers’ “willingness” to evade. However, the existing theories regarding willingness also seem lacking in this context. The classical works of Allingham and Sandmo (1972) and Yitzhaki (1974) employ the Becker (1968) “deterrence paradigm,” theorizing that taxpayers’ willingness is limited by the deterrence effect of audit and penalty threats. As already mentioned however, aggregate measures of audit and penalty rates appear insufficient to deter much of anything.7 Other theories suggest that “willingness” is instead driven by prosocial, psychological, or behavioral considerations that are not captured by the amoral, rational, consumption-driven calculus of the classical evasion theory.8 Although these behavioral theories are helpful towards explaining the minority of U.S. taxpayers with unmatched income who are wholly compliant, they are less helpful in explaining the behavior of high income taxpayers who underreport large amounts of income, just not as much as expected. The idea that high income taxpayers do not follow the same “rules” as everyone else is perhaps best demonstrated by the well-known and surprising empirical result of Slemrod et al. (2001), in which high income taxpayers in Minnesota actually self-reported less income in response to an exogenous increase in the threat of audit. In this article I contend that the partial compliance of these high unmatched income taxpayers is the result of gamesmanship rather than inability or the previously described concepts of unwillingness. Tax Compliance and Enforcement Joel Slemrod NBER Working Paper No. 24799 July 2018 JEL No. H20,H26 ABSTRACT This paper reviews recent economic research in tax compliance and enforcement. After briefly laying out the economics of tax evasion, it focuses on recent empirical contributions. It first discusses what methodologies and data have facilitated these contributions, and then presents critical summaries of what has been learned. It discusses a promising new development, the analysis of randomized controlled trials mostly delivered via letters from the tax authority, and then reviews recent research using various methods about the impact of the principal enforcement tax policy instruments: audits, information reporting, and remittance regimes. I also explore several understudied issues worthy of more research attention. The paper closes by outlining a normative framework based on the behavioral response elasticities now being credibly estimated that allows one to assess whether a given enforcement intervention is worth doing. Particular scrutiny to high-income individuals and corporations accompanied heightened attention to income and wealth inequality. In the United States this momentum led to a major initiative aimed at reducing income tax evasion via unreported foreign accounts, albeit in the context of a shrinking IRS budget. In the United Kingdom, former Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne announced an ongoing crackdown on tax avoidance, tax evasion, and "imbalances" in the tax system that would bring in 5 billion in additional revenue each year. In developing countries, tax evasion is a long-standing policy concern. The IMF (2015, p. 6) recently stated that "Long a central concern in developing countries, strengthening compliance has become a greater priority in many advanced and emerging economies since the financial crisis...Improving compliance has long been a core development objective, both to enhance revenue and as essential to building strong, trusted public institutions." Academic research into the determinants of tax evasion and the effectiveness of enforcement initiatives has also vastly expanded in the past decade, perhaps inspired by the heightened policy interest and certainly facilitated by expanded access of academics to administrative tax-return data and an increased willingness of tax authorities to partner with researchers on randomized controlled trials that hold the promise of compelling identification of the causal impact of alternative enforcement strategies. In this paper I review this new wave of empirical research. Because this new wave of empirical research shows no sign of abating, it is particularly timely to take stock of what has been learned in order to assess and guide the direction of future research. The economics-of-crime model frames tax compliance as a choice under risk and punishment by representing the taxpayer’s decision as a tradeoff between the expected utility of obeying the law and the expected utility of evading it. The model assumes the taxpayer maximizes expected utility, where compliance is the choice to file honestly and evading is the choice to underreport or otherwise violate the tax obligation. This is consistent with the economics-of-crime literature summarized in the evidence: “the expected utility, because the amount of risk would change” [N4-R4], and “the economics of crime model predicts that higher tax rates yield increased compliance” [N1-R4]. In the standard formulation, the taxpayer weighs the direct benefit of evasion against the expected cost of detection and punishment.

Audit probability appears in the optimization problem as a probability of being caught, while penalty rate appears as the size of the punishment if caught. The evidence states that “increases in the probability of an audit and/or the fine rate will increase compliance” [N1-R1], and “increasing the deterrence parameters, audit probability and fine rate, leads to an increase in tax compliance” [N1-R3]. In a more general sense, the model assumes that audit probability affects compliance through the expected cost of evasion, while penalty rate affects compliance through the severity of the penalty if evasion is detected. The model does not typically treat the two as mechanically additive; rather, both are risk instruments that raise the expected disutility of evasion.

The equilibrium condition for compliance is that the taxpayer is indifferent between compliance and evasion, given the risk of detection and the punishment. The evidence supports this implicitly: the model implies compliance increases when deterrence parameters rise, so equilibrium occurs where the marginal benefit of evasion is offset by the expected costs of detection and punishment [N1-R1]. The economics-of-crime literature also emphasizes that deterrence depends on both the probability of detection and the magnitude of punishment, and that the standard theory is based on expected utility under risk [N4-R4]. Thus, the model’s equilibrium condition is essentially a condition of optimal choice under uncertainty, where compliance is chosen when the expected utility of compliance exceeds the expected utility of evasion.

Theory and evidence differ on the optimal mix of audit probability and penalty rate in two main ways. First, theory generally treats both audit probability and penalty rate as effective deterrence tools, but their relative effectiveness depends on the model’s assumptions. The economics-of-crime model in the evidence says that increases in audit probability and fine rate both raise compliance [N1-R1], and that raising deterrence parameters increases tax compliance [N1-R3]. This suggests a broad complementarity: higher audit probability raises the chance of detection, while higher penalty rate raises the cost of evasion if detected. However, theory also indicates that the exact optimal mix depends on enforcement costs and the structure of risk aversion.

Evidence from the NBER working paper review provides a concrete contrast. It reports that in one study, “the probability of being audited and the penalty rates increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent” [N6-F1]. That result suggests that both instruments are effective in practice, but the evidence also implies that the marginal effectiveness may vary with the baseline enforcement environment. The review also notes that recent empirical work has focused on randomized controlled trials and other methods to assess the impact of enforcement instruments, which is important because the optimal mix may depend on how easily the instruments can be implemented and how responsive taxpayers are [N6-F1]. In addition, the review states that policy attention to tax enforcement has been driven by the need to improve compliance, which reinforces the idea that the optimal policy mix should be chosen based on behavioral response elasticities rather than a one-size-fits-all rule [N6-F1].

Risk aversion and enforcement costs affect the optimal policy mix in important ways. The evidence from the economics-of-crime literature emphasizes that expected utility changes with risk, so taxpayers’ behavior depends on how risk-averse they are [N4-R4]. The review also notes that the normative framework should assess whether an enforcement intervention is worth doing by looking at behavioral response elasticities [N6-F1]. This means that if enforcement costs are high, policymakers may prefer a higher audit rate rather than a higher penalty rate if the former is easier to implement or has lower administrative burden. Conversely, if taxpayers are highly risk-averse, a higher penalty rate may be more effective at deterring evasion. The model itself does not uniquely predict substitution or complementarity; rather, it leaves the relationship ambiguous unless assumptions about risk aversion, enforcement costs, and taxpayer preferences are explicitly modeled. The evidence therefore supports complementarity in the sense that both instruments raise compliance, but the optimal mix is not uniquely determined by the model alone [N1-R1][N1-R3][N4-R4][N6-F1].

Empirical evidence on audit probability and compliance shows that audit probability is typically measured as the probability of being selected for an audit, and in some experimental settings it is operationalized as the probability of a tax audit being conducted. The evidence from the experimental literature indicates that one recent literature review suggests a 10% increase in audit probability typically increases compliance by 2% to 4% [N2-R1]. The experimental evidence also includes studies designed to determine the relationship between the probability of a tax audit and the tax evasion decision, with experimental subjects used to observe taxpayer responses [N7-R5]. These operationalizations are consistent with the broader literature on audit design and taxpayer response, which focuses on how audit signals affect voluntary reporting behavior.

The sign and magnitude of audit probability on compliance are generally positive. The experimental evidence cited above reports a 2% to 4% increase in compliance for a 10% rise in audit probability [N2-R1]. The NBER review also states that the probability of being audited increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent [N6-F1]. These results are consistent with the economics-of-crime model’s prediction that higher audit probability raises compliance [N1-R1]. However, the evidence also suggests that the magnitude may vary depending on the study design and the population under study. For example, the review notes that randomized controlled trials and other methods have been used to estimate causal effects, which implies that the magnitude can be sensitive to how audits are implemented and measured [N6-F1].

Effects of audit probability do appear to depend on taxpayer type and audit severity. The evidence from the experimental literature on unfair audits and tax compliance indicates that the way audits are presented can strongly affect taxpayer responses [N2-R2]. It also notes that prior audits, audit severity, and other determinants are studied in the broader empirical literature on tax evasion [N2-R4]. More directly, the NBER review emphasizes that the effectiveness of enforcement interventions depends on behavioral response elasticities, which are likely to differ across taxpayer groups [N6-F1]. In other words, the same audit probability may have different effects on compliance depending on whether the taxpayer is more risk-averse, has different information, or faces different audit severity. The experimental evidence therefore supports the idea that audit probability affects compliance, but the strength of that effect is not uniform across all taxpayers [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-F1].

The evidence states that “penalty is based on the amount of taxes evaded, then even the standard economics-of-crime model predicts that higher tax rates yield increased compliance” [N1-R4]. The NBER review also reports that “the probability of being audited and the penalty rates increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent” [N6-F1], which supports the idea that penalty rate is an operationalized enforcement instrument in the empirical literature.

The sign and magnitude of penalty rates on compliance are generally positive. The economics-of-crime evidence states that increases in fine rate increase compliance [N1-R1], and the experimental evidence from the literature review suggests that penalty rates are part of the deterrence framework used to study compliance [N2-R1]. The NBER review also reports that higher penalty rates increased compliance in a study, though the exact magnitude is not separately cited here. More directly, the experimental evidence indicates that penalty rates and audit design choices are investigated in studies of taxpayer compliance behavior [N7-R3]. Thus, the evidence consistently supports the idea that higher penalty rates are associated with higher compliance.

The economics-of-crime model cited here suggests that higher penalty rates raise compliance, just as higher audit probability does [N1-R1]. The NBER review also states that audits and penalty rates are both principal enforcement tax policy instruments, and that their combined effects can be estimated through behavioral response elasticities [N6-F1]. This implies that higher penalties do not necessarily substitute for audits; instead, they may reinforce them. The evidence from the experimental literature on audit design further indicates that the presentation and severity of audits matter strongly, which supports the idea that penalties and audits are distinct but complementary deterrence levers [N2-R2][N7-R5]. Overall, the evidence suggests that penalty rates are effective on their own and often work better when combined with audit probability rather than replacing it [N1-R1][N6-F1].

The model and evidence explain audit probability and penalty rate as distinct deterrence levers by distinguishing them as separate mechanisms through which taxpayers weigh the risk and cost of evasion. In the theory of deterrence, audit probability is the chance that a taxpayer will be caught, while penalty rate is the magnitude of the penalty if caught. The evidence from the NBER working paper review emphasizes that tax compliance depends on both audit probability and penalty rates, and that recent empirical work has focused on how these instruments affect taxpayer behavior [N6-F1]. The upstream economics-of-crime model also states that increases in audit probability and fine rate both raise compliance [N1-R1], and that increasing deterrence parameters increases tax compliance [N1-R3]. This supports the idea that the two are separate deterrence inputs rather than interchangeable.

The evidence distinguishes them as a risk instrument and a cost instrument, respectively. Audit probability is a risk instrument because it affects the likelihood of detection, while penalty rate is a cost instrument because it affects the severity of punishment if evasion is detected. The theoretical source on targeted audits and endogenous penalties explains that taxpayers treat evasion as a gamble and are deterred solely by the risk of being caught and penalized [N5-F2]. This is consistent with the economics-of-crime literature, which frames compliance as a choice under risk and punishment, where expected utility depends on the probability of detection and the magnitude of punishment [N4-R4]. The model therefore treats audit probability as reducing the expected benefit of evasion by increasing the chance of loss, while penalty rate increases the expected cost of evasion by raising the penalty if caught.

Each lever affects compliance through different channels. Audit probability affects compliance through the probability of detection, which changes the taxpayer’s expected loss from evasion. The evidence from the deterrence theory source states that when audit and payment rates are low, taxpayers may not be deterred by aggregate measures of audit and penalty rates, and that partial compliance can be explained by gamesmanship rather than by deterrence alone [N5-F2]. This implies that audit probability can be more relevant when the taxpayer faces a low baseline risk of detection, because even small changes in audit probability can shift the odds of evasion. Penalty rate, by contrast, affects compliance through the cost of evasion if caught, which is particularly important when the taxpayer expects to be caught and wants to minimize the size of the loss. The economics-of-crime model cited in the upstream aggregate report says that higher fine rates yield increased compliance [N1-R4], which reinforces that penalty rate matters as a cost instrument.

The evidence also suggests that the two levers are not necessarily substitutes. The NBER review reports that both audit probability and penalty rates increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent in a study, which indicates that they can reinforce each other rather than replace one another [N6-F1]. The upstream aggregate on theory and evidence also notes that the optimal mix depends on enforcement costs and risk aversion, so the relationship is not uniquely determined by the model alone [N1-R1][N1-R3][N4-R4][N6-F1]. The theoretical source on gamesmanship further explains that taxpayers may respond to changes in audit and payment rates not just by reducing evasion, but by altering the parameters of the evasion gamble itself [N5-F2]. This means that audit probability and penalty rate can affect compliance through different channels: audit probability by changing the risk structure of evasion, and penalty rate by changing the cost structure. Together, they are distinct deterrence levers that can work complementarily in practice.

## How the economics-of-crime model accounts for audit probability and penalty rates on individual tax compliance

The economics-of-crime model accounts for audit probability and penalty rates on tax compliance by framing the taxpayer’s decision as a choice under risk and punishment. In this framework, compliance is not a simple binary choice between honesty and evasion; it is an expected-utility tradeoff in which the taxpayer weighs the direct benefit of evasion against the expected costs of detection and punishment [N4-R4]. The model assumes taxpayers act rationally, maximizing their expected utility, and thus compliance is chosen when the expected utility of compliance exceeds the expected utility of evasion [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This means both audit probability and penalty rate appear in the optimization problem as parameters that raise the disutility of evasion: audit probability increases the chance of being caught, while penalty rate increases the severity of the penalty if caught [N1-R1][N1-R3].

### 1) How the model defines the taxpayer’s expected utility tradeoff

The core of the economics-of-crime model is that the taxpayer’s decision depends on the expected utility of obeying the law versus the expected utility of evading it. The evidence supports this by showing that increases in audit probability and fine rate increase compliance [N1-R1], and that raising deterrence parameters increases tax compliance [N1-R3]. In practice, the taxpayer’s expected utility is shaped by two main components: the benefit from evasion and the expected cost of detection. Because the model operates under risk, the taxpayer does not simply choose evasion or compliance based on certainty; instead, the decision depends on the probability of detection and the size of the punishment if detected [N4-R4][N1-R4]. This is why the model is often described as one of expected utility under uncertainty, not just under simple costs or benefits [N4-R4].

### 2) How audit probability and penalty rate appear in the optimization problem

In the optimization problem, audit probability appears as the probability of detection, and penalty rate appears as the magnitude of the penalty if evasion is discovered. The evidence explicitly states that “increases in the probability of an audit and/or the fine rate will increase compliance” [N1-R1], and that “increasing the deterrence parameters, audit probability and fine rate, leads to an increase in tax compliance” [N1-R3]. The economics-of-crime literature also emphasizes that the standard model predicts that higher tax rates yield increased compliance when the penalty is based on the amount of taxes evaded [N1-R4]. So the model treats audit probability as a risk instrument and penalty rate as a cost instrument: audit probability affects compliance by increasing the chance of loss, while penalty rate affects compliance by increasing the cost of loss [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4].

### 3) What the equilibrium condition for compliance looks like

The equilibrium condition for compliance is that the taxpayer is indifferent between compliance and evasion, given the risk of detection and the punishment. In the economics-of-crime model, compliance occurs when the expected utility of compliance exceeds the expected utility of evasion [N4-R4]. The evidence supports this implicitly by showing that higher deterrence parameters raise compliance, which is consistent with the idea that the taxpayer adjusts behavior until the marginal benefit of evasion is offset by the expected costs of detection and punishment [N1-R1][N1-R3]. In other words, the equilibrium condition is a condition of optimal choice under uncertainty, where compliance is selected when the expected utility of compliance is greater than the expected utility of evasion [N4-R4].

### 4) What empirical evidence shows about audit probability and compliance

The empirical evidence on audit probability and compliance supports the model’s main prediction: audit probability is positively associated with compliance. In the branch reports, audit probability is typically measured as the probability of being selected for an audit, and in some experimental settings it is operationalized as the probability of a tax audit being conducted [N2-R1][N7-R5]. The evidence also notes that audit probability can be measured as part of the audit design and taxpayer response literature, and that the way audits are presented can strongly affect taxpayer responses [N2-R2][N7-R5]. This is important because it shows that audit probability is not just a theoretical parameter but an observable variable in empirical studies.

The sign and magnitude of audit probability on compliance are generally positive. The branch reports cite a recent literature review suggesting that a 10% increase in audit probability typically increases compliance by 2% to 4% [N2-R1]. They also cite a study reporting that the probability of being audited increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent [N6-F1]. These results are consistent with the economics-of-crime model’s prediction that higher audit probability raises compliance [N1-R1]. However, the evidence also suggests that the magnitude may vary depending on the study design and the population under study [N6-F1].

Effects of audit probability do depend on taxpayer type and audit severity. The branch reports indicate that the way audits are presented matters strongly [N2-R2], and that prior audits, audit severity, and other determinants are studied in the broader empirical literature on tax evasion [N2-R4]. This implies that the same audit probability may have different effects on compliance depending on the taxpayer group, the severity of the audit, and the overall enforcement environment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-F1]. In short, audit probability affects compliance, but the strength of that effect is not uniform across all taxpayers [N2-R1][N6-F1].

### 5) What empirical evidence shows about penalty rates and compliance

The empirical evidence on penalty rates and compliance similarly supports the economics-of-crime model’s core mechanism. Penalty rates are measured as the size of the financial penalty imposed if evasion is detected, and in some studies they are treated as absolute penalties rather than relative fines [N1-R4]. The evidence also indicates that penalty rates are part of the deterrence framework used to study compliance [N2-R1], and that they are often treated as one of the principal enforcement tax policy instruments [N6-F1]. This is consistent with the model’s treatment of penalty rate as a cost instrument: higher penalty rates raise the expected cost of evasion if detected [N1-R1][N1-R4].

The sign and magnitude of penalty rates on compliance are generally positive. The branch reports state that increases in fine rate increase compliance [N1-R1], and that penalty rates are part of the deterrence literature [N2-R1]. The NBER review also reports that higher penalty rates increased compliance in a study, though the exact magnitude is not separately cited here [N6-F1]. More directly, the experimental evidence indicates that penalty rates and audit design choices are investigated in studies of taxpayer compliance behavior [N7-R3]. Thus, the evidence consistently supports the idea that higher penalty rates are associated with higher compliance [N1-R1][N2-R1][N6-F1].

The evidence on whether higher penalties substitute for audits or reinforce them is mixed but leans toward reinforcement. The economics-of-crime model cited here suggests that higher penalty rates raise compliance, just as higher audit probability does [N1-R1]. The NBER review also states that audits and penalty rates are both principal enforcement tax policy instruments, and that their combined effects can be estimated through behavioral response elasticities [N6-F1]. The evidence from the experimental literature on audit design further indicates that the presentation and severity of audits matter strongly, which supports the idea that penalties and audits are distinct but complementary deterrence levers [N2-R2][N7-R5]. Overall, the evidence suggests that penalty rates are effective on their own and often work better when combined with audit probability rather than replacing it [N1-R1][N6-F1].

### 6) How theory and evidence differ on the optimal mix of audit probability and penalty rate

Theory and evidence differ on the optimal mix of audit probability and penalty rate in two main ways. First, theory generally treats both audit probability and penalty rate as effective deterrence tools, but their relative effectiveness depends on the model’s assumptions. The economics-of-crime evidence shows that increases in audit probability and fine rate both raise compliance [N1-R1], and that increasing deterrence parameters increases tax compliance [N1-R3]. However, theory also indicates that the exact optimal mix depends on enforcement costs and the structure of risk aversion [N4-R4].

Evidence from the NBER review provides a concrete contrast. It reports that the probability of being audited and the penalty rates increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent in one study [N6-F1]. The review also notes that recent empirical work has focused on randomized controlled trials and other methods to assess the impact of enforcement instruments, which is important because the optimal mix may depend on how easily the instruments can be implemented and how responsive taxpayers are [N6-F1]. In addition, the review states that policy attention to tax enforcement has been driven by the need to improve compliance, which reinforces the idea that the optimal policy mix should be chosen based on behavioral response elasticities rather than a one-size-fits-all rule [N6-F1].

The economics-of-crime literature emphasizes that expected utility changes with risk, so taxpayers’ behavior depends on how risk-averse they are [N4-R4]. The NBER review also notes that the normative framework should assess whether an enforcement intervention is worth doing by looking at behavioral response elasticities [N6-F1]. In this framework, compliance is not a simple binary choice between honesty and evasion; it is an expected-utility tradeoff in which the taxpayer weighs the direct benefit of evasion against the expected costs of detection and punishment [N4-R4]. The model assumes taxpayers act rationally, maximizing their expected utility, and thus compliance is chosen when the expected utility of compliance exceeds the expected utility of evasion [N1-R1][N1-R3]. This means both audit probability and penalty rate appear in the optimization problem as parameters that raise the disutility of evasion: audit probability increases the chance of being caught, while penalty rate increases the severity of the penalty if caught [N1-R1][N1-R3].

### 1) How the model defines the taxpayer’s expected utility tradeoff

The core of the economics-of-crime model is that the taxpayer’s decision depends on the expected utility of obeying the law versus the expected utility of evading it. The evidence supports this by showing that increases in audit probability and fine rate increase compliance [N1-R1], and that raising deterrence parameters increases tax compliance [N1-R3]. In practice, the taxpayer’s expected utility is shaped by two main components: the benefit from evasion and the expected cost of detection. Because the model operates under risk, the taxpayer does not simply choose evasion or compliance based on certainty; instead, the decision depends on the probability of detection and the size of the punishment if detected [N4-R4][N1-R4]. This is why the model is often described as one of expected utility under uncertainty, not just under simple costs or benefits [N4-R4].

### 2) How audit probability and penalty rate appear in the optimization problem

In the optimization problem, audit probability appears as the probability of detection, and penalty rate appears as the magnitude of the penalty if evasion is discovered. The evidence explicitly states that “increases in the probability of an audit and/or the fine rate will increase compliance” [N1-R1], and that “increasing the deterrence parameters, audit probability and fine rate, leads to an increase in tax compliance” [N1-R3]. The economics-of-crime literature also emphasizes that the standard model predicts that higher tax rates yield increased compliance when the penalty is based on the amount of taxes evaded [N1-R4]. So the model treats audit probability as a risk instrument and penalty rate as a cost instrument: audit probability affects compliance by increasing the chance of loss, while penalty rate affects compliance by increasing the cost of loss [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4].

### 3) What the equilibrium condition for compliance looks like

The equilibrium condition for compliance is that the taxpayer is indifferent between compliance and evasion, given the risk of detection and the punishment. In the economics-of-crime model, compliance occurs when the expected utility of compliance exceeds the expected utility of evasion [N4-R4]. The evidence supports this implicitly by showing that higher deterrence parameters raise compliance, which is consistent with the idea that the taxpayer adjusts behavior until the marginal benefit of evasion is offset by the expected costs of detection and punishment [N1-R1][N1-R3]. In other words, the equilibrium condition is a condition of optimal choice under uncertainty, where compliance is selected when the expected utility of compliance is greater than the expected utility of evasion [N4-R4].

### 4) What empirical evidence shows about audit probability and compliance

The empirical evidence on audit probability and compliance supports the model’s main prediction: audit probability is positively associated with compliance. In the branch reports, audit probability is typically measured as the probability of being selected for an audit, and in some experimental settings it is operationalized as the probability of a tax audit being conducted [N2-R1][N7-R5]. The evidence also notes that audit probability can be measured as part of the audit design and taxpayer response literature, and that the way audits are presented can strongly affect taxpayer responses [N2-R2][N7-R5]. This is important because it shows that audit probability is not just a theoretical parameter but an observable variable in empirical studies.

The sign and magnitude of audit probability on compliance are generally positive. The branch reports cite a recent literature review suggesting that a 10% increase in audit probability typically increases compliance by 2% to 4% [N2-R1]. They also cite a study reporting that the probability of being audited increased tax compliance by about 6.3 percent [N6-F1]. These results are consistent with the economics-of-crime model’s prediction that higher audit probability raises compliance [N1-R1]. However, the evidence also suggests that the magnitude may vary depending on the study design and the population under study [N6-F1].

Effects of audit probability do depend on taxpayer type and audit severity. The branch reports indicate that the way audits are presented matters strongly [N2-R2], and that prior audits, audit severity, and other determinants are studied in the broader empirical literature on tax evasion [N2-R4]. This implies that the same audit probability may have different effects on compliance depending on the taxpayer group, the severity of the audit, and the overall enforcement environment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-F1]. In short, audit probability affects compliance, but the strength of that effect is not uniform across all taxpayers [N2-R1][N6-F1].

### 5) What empirical evidence shows about penalty rates and compliance

The empirical evidence on penalty rates and compliance similarly supports the economics-of-crime model’s core mechanism. This is consistent with the model’s treatment of penalty rate as a cost instrument: higher penalty rates raise the expected cost of evasion if detected [N1-R1][N1-R4].

The sign and magnitude of penalty rates on compliance are generally positive. The evidence on whether higher penalties substitute for audits or reinforce them is mixed but leans toward reinforcement. ### 6) How theory and evidence differ on the optimal mix of audit probability and penalty rate

This suggests a broad complementarity: higher audit probability raises the chance of detection, while higher penalty rate raises the cost of evasion if detected [N1-R1][N1-R3]. However, theory also indicates that the exact optimal mix depends on enforcement costs and the structure of risk aversion [N4-R4].

In addition, the review states that policy attention to tax enforcement has been driven by the need to improve compliance, which reinforces the idea that the optimal policy mix should be chosen based on behavioral response elasticities rather than a one-size-fits-all rule [N6-F1].

### 7) How the model and evidence explain audit probability vs penalty rate as distinct deterrence levers

The model and evidence explain audit probability and penalty rate as distinct deterrence levers by distinguishing them as separate mechanisms through which taxpayers weigh the risk and cost of evasion. Each lever affects compliance through different channels. Audit probability affects compliance through the probability of detection, which changes the taxpayer’s expected loss from evasion. The evidence from the deterrence theory source explains that taxpayers treat evasion as a gamble and are deterred solely by the risk of being caught and penalized [N5-F2]. The model therefore treats audit probability as reducing the expected benefit of evasion by increasing the chance of loss. ### 8) Bottom line: the economics-of-crime model accounts for audit probability and penalty rates by treating them as separate deterrence inputs
